notes.meaning: The king and Haman arrived to dine with Queen Esther at her second banquet. In Persian royal custom, this was a private gathering centered around drinking wine. Esther used this quiet meal to bring her urgent plea directly to the king.

For the third time, the king urged Esther to tell him what she wanted, promising her anything up to half his realm. He knew these banquets were meant to prepare the way for an important request. His repeated promise gave her the opening and confidence she needed.

Esther asked the king to spare her life and the lives of her people as her only petition. Rather than asking for wealth or royal honors, she revealed that she was in mortal danger. This personal appeal touched the king deeply and prepared him to defend her.

Esther echoed the exact words of the royal decree to show that her people faced complete slaughter. She noted that if they had merely been sold into slavery she would have kept quiet, but no amount of money could repay the king for the total destruction of her people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Latin and Douay-Rheims translation translates the final sentence differently, stating that the enemy's cruelty would bring harm directly upon the king.

notes.meaning: King Xerxes asked in shock and fury who would dare to plan such an evil deed against his queen. His hurried questions showed how agitated he was. He was horrified by the plot, even though he had earlier signed Haman's decree without understanding what it meant.

Esther pointed straight at Haman and named him as the wicked enemy who planned their ruin. Haman was instantly struck with terror before the royal couple. He realized the queen was his prosecutor, the king was his judge, and his own conscience condemned him.

Boiling with rage, the king walked out into the palace garden to calm down and decide how to punish Haman. Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for mercy. He understood that the king's sudden exit signaled that his death had already been decided.

When the king returned from the garden, he found Haman falling across Esther's dining couch to beg for his life. The king treated this serious breach of royal space as an attack on the queen's honor. Royal attendants immediately covered Haman's face, showing he was condemned to die.

Harbonah, one of the palace servants, pointed out the seventy-five-foot gallows Haman had built at his own house for Mordecai. Hearing that the pole was made for the man who had saved his life, the king ordered Haman to be executed on it instead.

The palace guards executed Haman on the very pole he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's fury finally subsided. This sudden reversal showed God's justice at work, causing the plotter to be trapped by his own evil scheme.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The Greek version of Esther included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles explicitly credits God with changing the king's mind and records that Haman was hanged at the gates of Susa with his family.
